blocks.text: The Raven.
עורב (B. Kama 92b), fem. עורבתא (Sabbat 67b) and פושקנצא (B. batra 73b), for which Aruch has פשקנצא.
Because of its croaking (§. 38) it is also called: קורקיר (Baba batra 23a); because of its colour: עורב אוכמא (Chulin 63a).

Ravens love one another (Pesachim 113b), but (according to an old but erroneous notion) are without affection toward their young*), as long as these have not yet grown black feathers (Ketuboth 49b). As is well known, the young remain naked over the whole body for quite a long time (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 156). According to the Tosephot (ibid.)

[p. 173] that lack of affection is, however, said to be the case only with the common raven (§. 206), but not with the magpie (§. 210). Now since this latter kind of raven loves and feeds its young, one would call out to a man who will not feed his children: "He is worse than a raven!" (ibid.), just as one now says of a hard-hearted man: "He has a raven's heart!"

Meanwhile Providence cares for the young ravens, in that maggots arise from their own filth, on which they feed (B. batra 8a); the maggots even crawl into the ravens' mouths by themselves (Erubin 22a, cf. §. 470).

The adult ones feed on arum (Sabbat 126b*), as well as on fruits of trees and of the ground (Chulin 134b); that ravens seek out and devour the crops is also reported by Pliny (h. n. 17, 5, 4). They are attracted by blood (by the smell?), even by human blood, as on the occasion of bloodletting (B. batra 23a).
Of a black-haired youth it was customary to say: His locks are like the plumage of the raven (Chagigah 14a).

It also mates with the starling, since the latter belongs to its kind (B. Kama 92b**). During mating a mass of saliva flows from the mouth of the male into that of the female, and this is said to bring about fertilization (Sanhedrin 108b***).
If, in overcast weather, one wishes to know exactly when evening twilight begins, one should, when in the field, observe the ravens, which seek their night's roost at this time (Sabbat 35b).

The rich used to raise it as a domestic bird (ibid. 126b), but because of its filth it was kept away from the Temple at Jerusalem, which was accomplished by means of a scarecrow (Menachoth 107a). According to Aruch it was a figure such as gardeners are accustomed to make; Rashi explains the word כליה, as that scarecrow was called, as pointed pillars that were fixed on the Temple roof; the (so-called) Rashi commentary on M. Katan 9a explains it differently†).
The [p. 174] raven's croaking (§. 38) served superstition as an omen (Sabbat 67b). Cf. §. 249.
The Common Raven.

This splendidly black bird seems to be meant in the Talmud passages cited in the preceding article (Chulin 63a and Ketuboth 49b) by עורבא אוכמא "black raven"; perhaps the Tosephot (Chulin 62a s.v. מפני) also mean it when they call it קורביל, Corbeau. It has an אצבע יתירה, see on this §. 193, and a crop.
All the statements mentioned in the preceding article also apply to this one.
The Sea Raven.
The Hebrew שלך (Lev. 11, 17) is explained by the Talmud (Chulin 63a) as: השולה דגים מן הים "which draws the fish out of the sea"; Rashi adds: והוא עורב המים "it is the water raven".
Onkelos on the above biblical passage therefore translates שלך by שלינונא "fish-lifter".

This is the cormorant, which is called Corvus marinus (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 414). Pliny (h. n. 10, 48, 68) calls the bird Phalacorax, which Harduin, though apparently incorrectly, identifies with Corvo aquatico (§. 209). Voigt describes the bird thus: The bill narrow, straight, with a hook at the end. The bird is trained for fishing by placing a ring around its neck, so that it cannot swallow the fish it catches and must spit them out. It is common on the Baltic. However, the Talmud seems to mean another species of this bird, for this bird also lives in China, and is called Louwa there, see Iselin's Historische Lexicon part 1 s.v. Cining. The bird is described there: It has a very long neck and a hooked bill like an eagle, it is as large as a goose and looks not unlike a raven. The training and the use of that ring are carried out there in the same way.
A Species of Raven.

Chulin 64a states that there is a species of raven whose eggs are similar to those of the dove, for which reason one may buy such eggs, which are pointed at one end and blunt at the other, only when one is certain that they are dove eggs.

From this, however, the species of bird can hardly be determined, for the eggs of all species of raven known to us already differ from dove eggs by their colour; they are mostly blue-green, brown-spotted, or olive-brown, whereas dove eggs are white. The 8 plates of egg illustrations by Oken give no information on the point in question, and only a complete collection of eggs might perhaps make its determination possible.
The Sea Crow.

קאת, which name is explained by קיק (Chulin 63a). Of it it is said (Sabbat 21a): We asked all seafarers, and they told us that in the coastal towns there is a bird called קיק. In Arabic the word of the same sound قِيق [qīq] means: crow, and Pliny calls the sea raven, or sea crow, Corvum aquaticum.
